lines: A producer can be told a record is durable, and still be wrong about it.
What that promise actually means depends entirely on whose acknowledgement it waited for before believing it.
A real toy leader crash makes that gap concrete: one acknowledgement choice loses records it believed were safe, and a stricter choice loses none of them.
Every replica of a partition keeps its own copy of the log, and they don't all move at the same pace.
Picture a leader on top, its followers underneath, and a single ruler running through all of them.
Each one has its own mark on that ruler, and right now those marks sit at different places.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
The leader's own mark sits furthest along that ruler. Every follower trails somewhere behind it.
Which single position should a reader actually be allowed to trust as committed: the leader's own mark, the slowest in-sync replica's mark, or just whichever follower happens to be quickest?
answer: The slowest in-sync replica's mark, not the leader's own.
Trusting the leader's own mark assumes the leader never fails — if it died the instant after writing, there would be nothing backing that write up at all.
And picking one quick follower ignores the rest of the in-sync group entirely, when the whole point is that every member of that group has to have it.

lines: Here's that same replica picture, with real positions behind it.
The leader has pushed furthest along its own copy. One follower trails a little behind it, another trails considerably further back.
The committed line sits exactly at that slowest follower's mark, nowhere near the leader's own — and that gap between them is precisely what a crash can expose.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal settles it.
A follower that was down comes back holding more in its own log than its own recorded line says is safe.
Is it fine for that follower to just trust its own recorded line and cut everything past it, or does it need to ask for something else first?
answer: It needs to ask for something else: the end position of the current leadership period, not its own recorded line.
A follower's own recorded line is always at least one round trip behind what it has actually fetched, so trusting it blindly can throw away a message that was never genuinely in question.

A bare position number alone can't tell the difference between caught up but unconfirmed, and genuinely holding data the leader never had — only that leadership-period marker can make that distinction.

lines: Here's exactly that choice, played out on a short two-message log.
Cut the log down to the follower's own recorded line, and the second message disappears — gone, even though it was never actually divergent.
Cut it down to the current leadership period's end position instead, and that same second message survives untouched.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal settles it.
Imagine network trouble knocks every follower out of the in-sync group, leaving only the former leader standing alone.
Classically, does that lone remaining replica keep accepting writes that were meant to wait for the whole in-sync group, or does it quietly stop?
answer: The old rule only ever checks whether the in-sync group is empty before letting the committed line keep moving — it never checks that group's size against any configured minimum.

Whether risky elections are allowed later is a completely separate decision about who gets to lead after a failure. It has nothing to do with whether a write was ever safe to accept in the first place.

lines: Here's that exact gap, run for real, under two different rules.
Under the rule that only checks the group isn't empty, writes made while the group is shrunk keep getting accepted — and every single one of them is later lost when that lone replica fails uncleanly.
Under a rule that also checks the group's size against a configured minimum, none of those writes are ever accepted in the first place, so none of them are lost either.
Every number shown so far came from one real run, happening just now, not a diagram drawn ahead of time.
The gap between the committed line and the leader's own furthest position.
The two different truncation outcomes for the same short log, and the loss counts under both rules for letting that committed line move.
So: a replica column racing toward a line that only ever moves at the pace of its slowest in-sync member, never the leader's own.
A truncation rule that trusts a leadership-period marker over a follower's own stale recollection of what was safe.
And a minimum that has to be actively checked before that committed line is allowed to move at all, not just assumed to hold.
